title: Historical environmental fluctuations and recent anthropogenic activities drive demographic trajectories across slightly but significantly differentiated scallop stocks
content:
Abstract
Whether and how organisms respond to environmental fluctuations and anthropogenic activities over historical and contemporary timescales is a central question in evolutionary biology and conservation genetics. Bivalve mollusks have high evolutionary, ecological, and economic interests but are frequently susceptible to natural and anthropogenic disturbances. Consequently, it is critical to accurately assess their genetic diversity and effective population size through time. However, illuminating dynamics in effective population size in bivalves is challenging due to the complexity in stock identification. To address this gap, we conducted population genomic and demographic analyses using whole genome sequencing data for six representative natural stocks of a commercially important marine bivalve, Zhikong scallop Chlamys farreri. We detect subtle but significant genetic differentiation between southern and northern groups that exhibit differential levels of genetic diversity. Reconstructed dynamics in effective population size reveal two extreme bottlenecks within historical and contemporary timeframes across all stocks. While the ancient one could be ascribed to the Calabrian cooling, the recent one was caused by overfishing. A rapid recovery in effective population size, which has been rarely documented in commercial species, was observed following the recent bottleneck. This population recovery could result from reduced fishing pressure that has been facilitated by aquaculture. As an alternative approach for scallop harvesting, aquaculture substantially alleviates fishing pressure and indirectly creates conditions for sustained population recovery following wild fishery collapses. As intensive farming expands, aquaculture exerts disturbances on natural stocks. These findings, while acquired from scallop, have broad implications for both fundamental and applied sciences in marine species. From an evolutionary perspective, historical dynamics in effective population size provides complementary genomic evidence for understanding species turnover on geological timescales. From an applied perspective, population genomic and demographic inferences can inform management, conservation, and exploitation of marine resources. Although many marine species experience high gene flow, distinct management units still exist and should be considered in practice. Moreover, dynamics in effective population size, which can reflect and forecast stock status, correlate well with overfishing and aquaculture. This observed correlation suggests effective population size as a promising critical genetic metric to guide fishery management and aquaculture practices.
